property_summary: For any caller who is the owner and any new address a (a != owner), after setOwner(a) succeeds, c.owner() must equal a; the mutant never updates owner, so for a != the deployer the assertion fails.

For any caller and any proposed owner, a call to setOwner either reverts or leaves c.owner() equal to the proposed owner; the mutant's setOwner succeeds without updating owner, so when the real owner sets a new owner the call succeeds but c.owner() stays unchanged.

For any address newOwner, calling setOwner(newOwner) from the current owner succeeds and makes c.owner() equal newOwner; the mutant returns success but never changes the owner, so c.owner() stays the deployer for any newOwner != deployer.

For any address newOwner, calling setOwner(newOwner) as the current owner must set the contract's owner to exactly newOwner; the buggy version instead sets owner to msg.sender, so it violates this whenever newOwner != msg.sender.

For any caller that is not the current owner, calling setOwner must leave c.owner() unchanged (the call reverts); the mutant lets any non-owner change the owner, so for some fuzzed non-owner caller and new owner, c.owner() differs from the reference.

Calling setOwner(newOwner) as the current owner must leave the owner exactly equal to the requested newOwner (for any fuzzed caller and target); the mutant instead overwrites owner with msg.sender, so whenever newOwner != caller the invariant breaks.

property_summary: Whenever the current owner calls setOwner(x), the owner afterwards is exactly x; the mutant instead sets owner to the caller, so for any x != caller the post-state diverges.

After the owner transfers ownership to address a, a itself must be able to perform an owner-only action (call setOwner again); in the mutant the modifier silently re-assigns ownership to the caller, so the previous owner's transfer never takes effect and a's subsequent owner-only call reverts.
Ownership transfers compose: after the current owner transfers to a, and a transfers to b, the owner must be b; the mutant's modifier rewrites owner to the caller, leaving owner == a whenever b != a.

For any fuzzed target address t distinct from the current owner, a legitimate owner call setOwner(t) must leave owner exactly t; the mutant's modifier overwrites owner with msg.sender, so after the call owner reverts to the caller instead of t whenever t != caller.

For any caller and any new owner, setOwner succeeds and changes c.owner() to the new owner only when the caller is the current owner; otherwise the call reverts and owner stays unchanged — the mutant inverts the check so non-owners succeed (breaking this for some caller) while owners revert.

For any caller equal to the current owner and any address, a successful setOwner call must return true; the mutant returns false, so the fuzzer finds an input (owner-initiated setOwner) where the returned success flag is false.
For any caller that is the owner, a successful call to setOwner with any address returns true; the mutant drops the named return so it returns false.

property_summary: For any admissible input, a call by the current owner to setOwner(newOwner) makes c.owner() equal exactly newOwner; the mutant instead always sets owner to the caller, so it breaks whenever newOwner != msg.sender.

For any caller that is the current owner and any proposed address, calling setOwner(_owner) must set the public owner to exactly _owner; the mutant instead overwrites it with msg.sender, so for any _owner != msg.sender the assertion c.owner() == _owner fails.

For any caller other than the initial owner, a call to setOwner must revert and leave c.owner() unchanged; the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so an arbitrary fuzzed actor can set owner to any fuzzed address, breaking the rule.
For any caller and any new owner, a successful setOwner call must return true (and the reference always does), but the mutant inserts `return false;` so it returns false, violating the rule.
